terms.definition: A mixture of two or more metals (or a metal and another element) combined to create a material with properties neither has alone, such as the tin-silver-copper mix used in lead-free solder.
A reusable prototyping board with a grid of push-fit sockets that lets components and jumper wires be connected and rearranged without soldering.
The tendency of a liquid to flow into narrow spaces without outside help, which is how solder wick draws up molten solder during desoldering.
An unbroken electrical path between two points, usually confirmed with a multimeter's continuity or beep test before trusting a joint.
Removing solder from a joint to free a component or correct a mistake, typically with solder wick, a solder sucker, or a hot air station.
A sudden, often invisible flow of static electricity between objects that can silently destroy sensitive parts like MOSFETs and integrated circuits.
A chemical cleaning agent, often built into the core of solder wire, that removes oxide from metal surfaces so molten solder can bond to them.
A chemical reaction in which a metal surface combines with oxygen, leaving a dull or crusty layer that blocks a good electrical or solder connection.
A measure of how strongly a material opposes the flow of electric current, measured in ohms; a good solder joint keeps this as low as the wire itself.
A solid resin, often derived from pine trees, used as the flux embedded in rosin-core solder to clean surfaces as they're heated.
The movement of fresh air through a space to carry away fumes, such as the flux smoke produced while soldering.
The way molten solder spreads smoothly across a clean, hot metal surface instead of beading up; good wetting is the sign of a sound joint.
